Tsushima|Japan.f: Tsushima was cut into two islands by a canal in 1671 and into three by a second canal in 1900.

Rishiri|Japan.f: Mount Rishiri rises 1,721 meters straight from the sea, and the island is noted for its dried kombu.

Izu Oshima|Japan.f: Izu Oshima is the largest and closest of Tokyo's outlying islands, and Mount Mihara's 1986 eruption forced an evacuation.

Okushiri|Japan.f: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake on 12 July 1993 sent a tsunami that killed 198 people in Okushiri town.

Yakushima|Japan.f: Yakushima is Japan's wettest place, with annual precipitation of 4,000 to 10,000 mm.

Minamidaito|Japan.f: Minamidaito, 360 km east of Okinawa Island, had no inhabitants until pioneers from Hachijojima arrived in 1900.

Kitadaito|Japan.f: Until World War II, the whole of Kitadaito was owned by Dai Nippon Sugar, which also mined guano there.

Tarama|Japan.f: Tarama got direct telephone service in 1964 and only five hours of power a day, rising to 17 hours by 1969.

Yonaguni|Japan.f: Yonaguni is Japan's westernmost municipality, 107.3 km from Taiwan and 118 km from Ishigaki.

Okinoerabu|Japan.f: Okinoerabu has an extensive limestone cave system in its east, described as one of the largest in Asia.

Miyakejima|Japan.f: Miyakejima was fully evacuated in 2000 after Mount Oyama erupted, and residents could only return permanently on 1 February 2005.

Yoron|Japan.f: Yoron has been a sister town of Mykonos, Greece, since 1985.

Iki|Japan.f: Iki is the eroded basaltic summit of a huge stratovolcano that was last active over 600,000 years ago.

Kikai|Japan.f: The Amami island of Kikai was under US administration from 1946 to 1953 and now lives on sugar cane, shochu and tourism.

Toyooka|Japan.f: Toyooka's oriental white storks went extinct in the wild in the 1970s, and by June 2015 there were 72 wild ones again.

Sado|Japan.f: The Sado Mine ran for nearly 400 years and produced 78 tons of gold and 2,300 tons of silver before closing in 1989.

Amakusa|Japan.f: Amakusa is the fastest depopulating city in Japan since 2005, falling from 96,473 people to 72,243 by August 2024.

Niijima|Japan.f: Niijima in the Izu Islands is known for sports fishing, hot spring resorts and its own local beer.

Aguni|Japan.f: Aguni's highest point is only 97.3 meters, and the island was home to merchants and mariners in the Ryukyu Kingdom's sailing era.
